q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which the British Empire expanded in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why Britain was able to build the largest empire of the nineteenth century, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which British imperial rule changed the economies of colonized regions in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.

sample_answers.a: Britain seized control of India from the Mughals and the East India Company, then expanded across Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific, so that by 1900 the empire covered a quarter of the world's land surface.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, Britain's early industrialization gave it the wealth, naval power, and military technology (such as steam gunboats and repeating rifles) to conquer and hold distant territories more effectively than any rival.
sample_answers.c: British policy reoriented colonial economies toward exporting raw materials (such as Indian cotton or Malayan rubber) and importing British manufactured goods, which undermined local industries like Indian textiles that could not compete with factory production.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the nineteenth-century British Empire as the largest the world had ever seen, encompassing a quarter of the earth's population by 1900. Its growth was driven by the interaction of industrial power and strategic ambition: Britain's factories needed raw materials and markets, its navy needed coaling stations and ports, and its statesmen feared that rivals would seize territories first. Yet the empire was not simply a product of strength; it also reflected the vulnerabilities of industrial Britain, which depended on imported food and raw materials and therefore sought political control over the sources of supply. The result was an empire that was simultaneously a source of immense wealth and a heavy burden, requiring constant military effort to maintain.
—Historian's account of the British Empire in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim the account makes about the significance of the Great Exhibition.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the Great Exhibition displayed Britain's imperial power.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the Great Exhibition's celebration of industry and empire ignored the costs of British power.

sample_answers.a: The account claims the Exhibition proved Britain's position as the 'workshop of the world,' displaying the industrial and imperial might that made Britain the leading global power.
sample_answers.b: Exhibitors from across the empire — India, Canada, Australia — displayed raw materials and crafts alongside British machinery, presenting the empire as a unified system in which colonies supplied resources and Britain supplied manufacturing genius.
sample_answers.c: The Exhibition was organized by Britain's elite to celebrate their own achievements; it had no reason to show the Indian weavers ruined by British textiles, the enslaved labor behind colonial products, or the wars of conquest that built the empire.

q2.stimulus:
The Crystal Palace, that marvellous structure of glass and iron, contains within its walls the industry of all nations, yet it is Britain that stands pre-eminent. Here the world may see the fruits of British ingenuity: the steam engines, the textile machinery, the ironwork that have made this small island the workshop of the world. The contributions from our colonies — the cotton of India, the wool of Australia, the timber of Canada — testify to the vastness of an empire upon which the sun never sets, and to the benefits which British rule confers upon distant lands.
—Adapted from a British newspaper account of the Great Exhibition, London, 1851

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the Crystal Palace that symbolized Britain's industrial power.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the Great Exhibition of 1851 reflected continuity in Britain's global economic role.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Great Exhibition reflected a change in how Britain presented its empire to the world.

sample_answers.a: The building itself — an enormous structure of mass-produced glass and iron, assembled with industrial precision — demonstrated Britain's mastery of the new materials and engineering techniques of the Industrial Revolution.
sample_answers.b: The Exhibition continued Britain's long-standing role as the center of global trade networks, a position it had held since the eighteenth century; the display of colonial raw materials alongside British manufactures reflected the ongoing imperial division of labor.
sample_answers.c: Earlier British power had been presented mainly through naval victories and territorial conquest, but the Exhibition presented empire as peaceful commerce and technological progress — a deliberate rebranding of domination as benevolent modernity for a mass audience.

q3.stimulus: The image is an 1851 illustration of the Crystal Palace, the giant glass-and-iron exhibition hall built in London's Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition of 1851. The first world's fair, it attracted over six million visitors and displayed manufactured goods and raw materials from Britain and its colonies. The building itself — 1,848 feet long, made of prefabricated iron and glass — was a triumph of industrial engineering and became an enduring symbol of Victorian Britain's confidence.
